public.prompt: A cell in the Orders sheet displays the text "Lagos". Which of the following best describes the difference between the cell's address and its contents?

options.text: The address is the column-letter/row-number label (e.g., B2) that identifies where the cell sits in the grid; the contents are the value stored inside it (e.g., "Lagos").
The address is the value stored in the cell (e.g., "Lagos"); the column letter and row number are just display labels.
The address and the contents are the same thing — both refer to the text "Lagos" shown in the cell.
The address is the row number only (e.g., 2); the column letter is part of the contents.

opt_b.message: That is reversed. The value "Lagos" is the cell's contents — what is stored inside it. The address is the column-letter/row-number label (like B2) that tells you where the cell lives in the grid.

opt_c.message: They are different things. The address (e.g., B2) is a fixed location label; the contents (e.g., "Lagos") are what you typed or calculated. You could change the contents without changing the address.

opt_d.message: A cell address includes both the column letter and the row number together (e.g., B2). Neither part alone is the address, and neither is part of the contents.

correct.message: Exactly right. The address (B2) is the fixed grid location; the contents ("Lagos") are the value stored there. You can change the contents without changing the address.

incorrect.message: The address is the column-letter/row-number label that locates the cell in the grid (e.g., B2). The contents are the value stored inside that cell (e.g., "Lagos"). They are two separate things.

hints: Think about what stays the same when you type something new into a cell — the location label or the value?
In Excel, the Name Box (top-left) shows the address; the cell itself shows the contents.

public.prompt: The QuickDeliver workbook has a sheet named Orders. In that sheet, column B holds the delivery city and row 2 holds the first order. Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the value stored at the intersection of column B and row 2.

correct.message: Correct! =B2 points at column B, row 2 — the first order's city in the Orders sheet. The address B2 is the column letter followed by the row number, exactly as the A1 reference style works.

incorrect.message: Remember: a cell address is the column letter followed by the row number. Column B, row 2 gives the address B2. Type =B2 to return the value stored there.

hints: The column letter comes first, then the row number — no space between them.
Start your formula with = so Excel knows it is a formula, not plain text.

public.prompt: New delivery orders are added to the Orders sheet every day, so the city column keeps growing. Which reference covers every cell in column B, no matter how many rows are added?

options.text: B:B
B1

opt_b.message: B2:B51 covers only rows 2 through 51. If a 52nd order is added, that row is outside the range. A whole-column reference like B:B always covers every row, past and future.

opt_c.message: B1 is a single-cell reference — it points at just one cell, the header row. It does not cover the rest of column B.

opt_d.message: B:2 is not valid range notation. A whole-column reference repeats the column letter on both sides of the colon: B:B. A whole-row reference repeats the row number: 2:2.

correct.message: Correct! B:B selects every cell in column B by repeating the column letter on both sides of the colon. It automatically includes any new rows added later.

incorrect.message: To reference an entire column, repeat the column letter on both sides of a colon: B:B. This covers every row in column B, including rows added in the future.

hints: A whole-column reference uses the same letter twice, separated by a colon.
Compare: 5:5 selects all of row 5; the same pattern with a letter selects all of a column.

public.prompt: The Orders sheet has 20 orders in rows 2 through 21. The delivery_minutes values are in column C. The range C2:C21 covers all the delivery_minutes values. In cell A1, type a formula that returns the value from the first cell in this range (the delivery_minutes value for the first order in row 2).

correct.message: Correct! =C2 references the first cell in the range C2:C21. A range reference like C2:C21 uses a colon to connect the starting cell (C2) and the ending cell (C21), covering all cells in between.

incorrect.message: The range C2:C21 starts at cell C2 (column C, row 2) and ends at C21 (column C, row 21). To reference the first cell in this range, type =C2.

hints: A range reference uses a colon between two cell addresses: start:end. The range C2:C21 starts at C2.
The first cell in a range is the cell address that appears before the colon.

public.prompt:
You type the following into cell D4 of the Orders sheet: D2+D3

What happens when you press Enter?

options.text: Excel treats it as text and displays the string "D2+D3" in the cell.
Excel adds the values in D2 and D3 and shows the numeric result.
Excel shows a #NAME? error because the cell addresses are invalid.
Excel shows a #VALUE! error because + requires numbers.

opt_b.message: Without a leading = Excel does not evaluate the entry as a formula. It stores the literal text "D2+D3" instead of computing a sum.

opt_c.message: #NAME? appears when Excel cannot recognise a name inside a formula. Here there is no formula at all — the entry has no = prefix, so Excel stores it as plain text.

opt_d.message: #VALUE! occurs when a formula receives the wrong type of argument. But without a leading = there is no formula to evaluate, so no error is raised — the entry is stored as text.

correct.message: Correct! Without the = prefix Excel treats the entry as plain text and displays "D2+D3" literally. Every formula must start with = to tell Excel to compute a value.

incorrect.message: Formulas in Excel always begin with the equal sign (=). Without it, Excel treats the entry as plain text and displays it as-is, not as a computed result.

hints: Think about what tells Excel that an entry is a formula rather than a label.
Try typing just the letter A in a cell — Excel shows 'A', not an error.

public.prompt:
Which formula correctly sums the range D2:D21 on the Orders sheet?

The Orders sheet has 20 rows of data in rows 2–21. You want to add up all the values in the amount column (D2:D21) using the SUM function. Which formula is correctly structured?

options.text: =SUM(D2:D21)
SUM(D2:D21)
=SUM D2:D21
=SUM(D2,D21)

opt_b.message: This is missing the = prefix. Without it, Excel stores the entry as text rather than evaluating the SUM function.

opt_c.message: The parentheses are required. The correct syntax is =SUM(range) — the opening parenthesis immediately follows the function name, and the range goes inside.

opt_d.message: =SUM(D2,D21) adds only two individual cells: D2 and D21. To sum a continuous range of cells, use the colon notation: D2:D21.

correct.message: Correct! =SUM(D2:D21) follows the required structure: = prefix, function name, opening parenthesis, the range D2:D21, closing parenthesis. This sums all 20 amount values.

incorrect.message: A function formula needs: = prefix, the function name, an opening parenthesis, the range argument, and a closing parenthesis — for example =SUM(D2:D21).

hints: Every formula starts with =. Then comes the function name, then the range inside parentheses.
D2:D21 uses a colon to mean 'from D2 to D21'. A comma would list only two separate cells.

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has order amounts in column D (rows 2–21). Row 2 (LG-2001) has amount **4500** and row 3 (LG-2002) has amount **7200**.

**Task 1 — subtraction:** In cell E1, write a formula that subtracts the amount in D2 from the amount in D3 (D3 minus D2). The result should be **2700**.

**Task 2 — operator precedence:** In cell E2, write a formula that first adds D2 and D3, then multiplies the sum by 2. Use parentheses to force the addition before the multiplication. The result should be **23400**.

tests.message_on_fail: E1 should equal 2700 (D3 minus D2 = 7200 - 4500). Make sure your formula starts with = and uses the - operator between D3 and D2.
E2 should equal 23400 ((D2+D3)*2 = (4500+7200)*2 = 11700*2). Without parentheses, =D2+D3*2 gives 18600 because * is evaluated before +. Wrap the addition in parentheses: =(D2+D3)*2.

correct.message: Well done! E1 uses = and the - operator to subtract D2 from D3, returning 2700. E2 uses parentheses to force the addition (D2+D3) before the multiplication by 2, returning 23400. Without parentheses, =D2+D3*2 would give 18600 because * has higher precedence than +.

incorrect.message: Check both cells. E1 needs =D3-D2 (the = prefix, then D3, then -, then D2). E2 needs parentheses around the addition: =(D2+D3)*2. Without parentheses, multiplication happens before addition and the result is wrong.

hints: Every formula must start with =. Without it, Excel stores the entry as text.
Parentheses change the order of operations: =(D2+D3)*2 adds first, then multiplies.

public.prompt:
You are building a multiplication table. Row 1 holds the column multipliers (B1, C1, D1, …) and column A holds the row multipliers (A2, A3, A4, …). You want to enter one formula in B2 and copy it across the entire table so that it always multiplies the correct row multiplier by the correct column multiplier.

Which formula should you enter in B2?

opt_b.message: $A$2 locks both the column and the row of the row multiplier. When you copy the formula down, the row part ($2) never changes, so every row in the table uses A2 instead of A3, A4, etc.

opt_c.message: =A2*B1 uses fully relative references. When copied across columns, A2 shifts to B2, C2, etc., so the formula no longer reads from column A. When copied down, B1 shifts to B2, B3, etc., losing the header row.

opt_d.message: $A$2 locks both dimensions of the row multiplier, so copying down always reads A2 instead of A3, A4, etc. You need $A2 (lock column A, let the row adjust) to keep the row multiplier in column A while allowing the row to change.

correct.message: Correct! =$A2*B$1 uses two mixed references. $A2 locks column A so the row multiplier always comes from column A, while the row number adjusts as you copy down. B$1 locks row 1 so the column multiplier always comes from row 1, while the column letter adjusts as you copy across.

incorrect.message: A mixed reference locks one dimension and lets the other adjust. $A2 locks the column (A stays fixed) but lets the row change when copied down. B$1 locks the row (1 stays fixed) but lets the column change when copied across. Together, =$A2*B$1 fills the entire multiplication table correctly from one formula.

hints: The $ sign locks the part that follows it: $A locks the column, $1 locks the row.
Ask yourself: when I copy this formula down, which part must NOT change? When I copy across, which part must NOT change?

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has order amounts in column D (rows 2–4). Cell H1 holds the tax rate **0.075** (7.5%).

**Task:** In cells E2, E3, and E4, write a formula that multiplies each row's amount (D2, D3, D4) by the shared tax rate in H1. Use an **absolute reference** for H1 so the tax-rate address does not change when the formula is copied down. Use a **relative reference** for the amount cell so it adjusts to the correct row.

- E2 should equal **337.5** (4500 × 0.075)
- E3 should equal **540** (7200 × 0.075)
- E4 should equal **232.5** (3100 × 0.075)

tests.message_on_fail: E2 should equal 337.5 (D2 × H1 = 4500 × 0.075). Use =D2*$H$1 — the $ signs lock H1 so it does not shift when copied.
E3 should equal 540 (D3 × H1 = 7200 × 0.075). If you copied =D2*$H$1 down, D2 should have adjusted to D3 while $H$1 stayed fixed.
E4 should equal 232.5 (D4 × H1 = 3100 × 0.075). Check that E4 uses D4 (relative, adjusts per row) and $H$1 (absolute, stays fixed).

correct.message: Excellent! =D2*$H$1 uses a relative reference for D2 (it adjusts to D3, D4 as you copy down) and an absolute reference for $H$1 (the $ signs lock both the column H and row 1, so the tax-rate cell never shifts). This is the key pattern for applying a shared rate to a column of values.

incorrect.message: Use =D2*$H$1 in E2. The $ signs in $H$1 lock the tax-rate cell so it does not shift when the formula is copied. D2 has no $ signs, so it adjusts to D3 in E3 and D4 in E4. If you used =D2*H1 (no $), H1 would shift to H2, H3, etc. when copied down.

hints: Add $ before both the column letter and the row number of H1 to lock it: $H$1.
Leave D2 without $ signs so it automatically becomes D3 when you copy the formula to E3.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has 20 rows. Column A holds order IDs (text like "LG-2001"), column C holds delivery_minutes (numbers for delivered orders, blank for pending/cancelled), and column D holds order amounts (all numbers).

A manager asks: "How many orders have a recorded delivery time?" Which function should you use, and why?

options.text: COUNT(C2:C21) — because COUNT counts only numeric cells and delivery_minutes is blank for undelivered orders.
COUNTA(C2:C21) — because COUNTA counts all non-empty cells, including text.
SUM(C2:C21) — because SUM adds up all the delivery times to give a total count.
AVERAGE(C2:C21) — because AVERAGE returns the number of values in the range.

opt_b.message: COUNTA counts any non-empty cell, including text. For delivery_minutes, all non-blank cells are numbers, so COUNTA and COUNT give the same result here. But COUNT is the precise choice: it counts only numeric cells, which is exactly what 'has a recorded delivery time' means.

opt_c.message: SUM adds the values together and returns a total number of minutes, not a count of rows. To count how many rows have a value, use COUNT or COUNTA.

opt_d.message: AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean of the values, not the number of values. To count how many cells contain a number, use COUNT.

correct.message: Correct! COUNT(C2:C21) counts only the numeric cells in the delivery_minutes column. Blank cells (for pending/cancelled orders) are skipped, so the result equals the number of orders with a recorded delivery time.

incorrect.message: COUNT counts only numeric cells and ignores blanks, text, and logical values. Because delivery_minutes is blank for undelivered orders, COUNT(C2:C21) returns exactly the number of orders that have a recorded delivery time.

hints: COUNT counts only numbers. COUNTA counts anything that is not empty. SUM adds values. AVERAGE computes a mean.
Blank cells in delivery_minutes represent orders with no recorded time — COUNT skips them automatically.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has 20 rows of data (rows 2–21). Column A holds order IDs — text values like "LG-2001". Column D holds order amounts — all numeric.

In cell H1, write a formula using **COUNTA** that counts how many non-empty cells are in the order_id column (A2:A21). Because order IDs are text, COUNT would return 0 — COUNTA is the right choice here.

The expected result is **20**.

correct.message: Correct! =COUNTA(A2:A21) returns 20 because all 20 order-ID cells are non-empty. COUNTA counts any non-empty cell — numbers, text, or errors — while COUNT counts only numeric cells. Since order IDs are text, COUNT(A2:A21) would return 0.

incorrect.message: Use =COUNTA(A2:A21). COUNTA counts every non-empty cell regardless of type, so it correctly counts the 20 text order IDs. COUNT would return 0 here because it only counts numeric cells.

hints: COUNTA counts cells that contain any value — numbers, text, or errors. COUNT counts only numbers.
The range A2:A21 covers all 20 data rows in column A (order_id).

public.prompt:
Cell C2 holds a delivery time in minutes. You want a formula in F2 that displays "Late" if the delivery took more than 60 minutes, or "On Time" otherwise.

Which formula is correct?

options.text: =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time")
=IF(C2>60,Late,On Time)
=IF("C2>60","Late","On Time")
=IF(C2>60,"On Time","Late")

opt_b.message: Text results in an IF formula must be enclosed in double quotation marks. Without quotes, Excel tries to interpret Late and On Time as cell names or named ranges and returns a #NAME? error.

opt_c.message: The logical_test (C2>60) must not be in quotes. Putting it in quotes makes Excel treat it as a text string rather than evaluating it as a comparison, so the condition is never tested.

opt_d.message: The arguments are in the wrong order. IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false): the second argument is returned when the condition is TRUE (C2>60), so "Late" must come second, not "On Time".

correct.message: Correct! =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time") tests whether C2 is greater than 60. If TRUE it returns the text "Late"; if FALSE it returns "On Time". Text values in formulas must always be wrapped in double quotation marks.

incorrect.message: The IF syntax is IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Text results must be in double quotes: "Late" and "On Time". The logical test (C2>60) must not be in quotes — it is a comparison, not text.

hints: Text in a formula always goes inside double quotation marks, like "Late".
The second argument of IF is what is returned when the condition is TRUE.

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has delivery times in column C (rows 2–5). You need to classify each delivery into one of three bands:

- **"Late"** if delivery_minutes > 60
- **"On Time"** if delivery_minutes is between 30 and 60 (inclusive on both ends)
- **"Fast"** if delivery_minutes < 30

**Task 1 — nested IF with AND:** In cell F2, write a nested IF formula that classifies the delivery time in C2. Use **AND** as the logical_test of the inner IF to enforce both the lower bound (>=30) and the upper bound (<=60) of the "On Time" band. Then write the same formula in F3 and F4.

Expected results:
- F2: **"Fast"** (C2 = 28)
- F3: **"Fast"** (C3 = 25)
- F4: **"On Time"** (C4 = 56)

**Task 2 — OR flag:** In cell F5, write an IF formula that returns **"Extreme"** if C5 is less than 20 **OR** greater than 70, and **"Normal"** otherwise. Use **OR** as the logical_test.

Expected result:
- F5: **"Extreme"** (C5 = 19)

solution_files.content:
// Input cells (typed constants):
orders!C2: 28
orders!C3: 25
orders!C4: 56
orders!C5: 19

// Formula cells:
F2: =IF(C2>60,"Late",IF(AND(C2>=30,C2<=60),"On Time","Fast"))
F3: =IF(C3>60,"Late",IF(AND(C3>=30,C3<=60),"On Time","Fast"))
F4: =IF(C4>60,"Late",IF(AND(C4>=30,C4<=60),"On Time","Fast"))
F5: =IF(OR(C5<20,C5>70),"Extreme","Normal")

tests.message_on_fail: F2 should be "Fast" because C2=28 is less than 30. Check the order of your IF conditions: test >60 first, then AND(>=30,<=60), then the else is Fast.
F3 should be "Fast" because C3=25 is less than 30. Check the order of your IF conditions: test >60 first, then AND(>=30,<=60), then the else is Fast.
F4 should be "On Time" because C4=56 is between 30 and 60. Use AND(C4>=30,C4<=60) as the logical_test of the inner IF.
F2 must use both IF and AND. Use AND(C2>=30,C2<=60) as the logical_test of the inner IF to enforce both bounds of the 'On Time' band.
F5 should be "Extreme" because C5=19 is less than 20. Use =IF(OR(C5<20,C5>70),"Extreme","Normal"). OR returns TRUE when any condition is met.
F5 must use both IF and OR. Use OR(C5<20,C5>70) as the logical_test: OR returns TRUE when any one of its conditions is TRUE.

correct.message: Well done! Your nested IF correctly classifies all three delivery times using AND for the On Time band. AND returns TRUE only when BOTH conditions are met. Your OR formula in F5 correctly flags C5=19 as Extreme because OR returns TRUE when ANY condition is met (19 < 20 is TRUE).

incorrect.message: For F2–F4: use =IF(C2>60,"Late",IF(AND(C2>=30,C2<=60),"On Time","Fast")). AND requires BOTH bounds to be true. For F5: use =IF(OR(C5<20,C5>70),"Extreme","Normal"). OR returns TRUE when ANY condition is true.

hints: Start with the outer IF: =IF(C2>60,"Late", ...). Then nest another IF for the middle band.
AND(C2>=30,C2<=60) returns TRUE only when C2 is at least 30 AND at most 60.

public.prompt: A colleague shares a workbook that uses =CONCATENATE(A2," ",B2) to join a first name and a last name. Which statement about CONCATENATE is accurate?

options.text: CONCATENATE works but Microsoft recommends using CONCAT instead, as CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel.
CONCATENATE is the current recommended function and CONCAT is the deprecated one.
CONCATENATE automatically skips empty cells, so no ignore_empty argument is needed.
CONCATENATE can only join two text strings at a time.

opt_b.message: This is reversed. Microsoft recommends the newer CONCAT function and notes that CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel.

opt_c.message: CONCATENATE does not skip empty cells — it joins them as blank values, which can produce unwanted extra spaces. TEXTJOIN with ignore_empty=TRUE is the function that skips empty cells.

opt_d.message: CONCATENATE accepts multiple text arguments: CONCATENATE(text1, [text2], ...). It can join more than two strings in a single formula.

correct.message: Correct! CONCATENATE joins text strings and its syntax is CONCATENATE(text1, [text2], ...). However, Microsoft recommends using the newer CONCAT function instead, since CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel.

incorrect.message: CONCATENATE joins two or more text strings. Microsoft recommends using CONCAT instead, as CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel. Neither function automatically skips empty cells — use TEXTJOIN with ignore_empty=TRUE for that.

hints: Think about which function Microsoft says is the newer, recommended replacement.
TEXTJOIN is the function with the ignore_empty argument, not CONCATENATE.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has the delivery city in column B and the order status in column E. Row 2 has city **"Lagos"** and status **"Delivered"**.

In cell H2, write a TEXTJOIN formula that combines the city (B2) and status (E2) with the delimiter **" | "** (space-pipe-space) and sets ignore_empty to **TRUE**.

The expected result is **"Lagos | Delivered"**.

correct.message: Correct! =TEXTJOIN(" | ",1 (or TRUE()),B2,E2) joins B2 ("Lagos") and E2 ("Delivered") with the delimiter " | ", returning "Lagos | Delivered". Setting ignore_empty to 1 (or TRUE()) means any blank cells in the argument list are skipped rather than producing an extra delimiter.

incorrect.message: Use =TEXTJOIN(" | ",1 (or TRUE()),B2,E2). The first argument is the delimiter (" | "), the second is ignore_empty (1 (or TRUE())), and the remaining arguments are the cells to join (B2 and E2). Make sure the delimiter is in double quotes.

hints: TEXTJOIN syntax: TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, [text2], ...)
The delimiter " | " includes spaces on both sides of the pipe character.

public.prompt:
Cell A2 contains the order ID **"LG-2001"**. You want to extract the 4-digit number starting at position 4 (the "2001" part).

Which formula correctly extracts exactly 4 characters starting at position 4?

options.text: =LEFT(A2,4)

opt_b.message: =MID(A2,4,3) starts at position 4 but extracts only 3 characters, returning "200" instead of "2001". The third argument of MID is the number of characters to extract.

opt_c.message: =LEFT(A2,4) extracts the first 4 characters from the left, returning "LG-2" instead of "2001". LEFT always starts from the beginning of the string.

opt_d.message: =MID(A2,3,4) starts at position 3, which is the "-" character in "LG-2001". This returns "-200" instead of "2001". The start position must be 4 to begin at the "2" character.

correct.message: Correct! =MID(A2,4,4) starts at position 4 (the "2" in "2001") and extracts 4 characters, returning "2001". MID syntax: MID(text, start_num, num_chars).

incorrect.message: MID(text, start_num, num_chars) extracts num_chars characters starting at start_num. In "LG-2001": position 1=L, 2=G, 3=-, 4=2, 5=0, 6=0, 7=1. To get "2001", start at position 4 and extract 4 characters: =MID(A2,4,4).

hints: Count the characters in "LG-2001": L=1, G=2, -=3, 2=4, 0=5, 0=6, 1=7.
MID's third argument is how many characters to return, not the end position.

public.prompt:
A city name imported from an external system is stored in cell B2 as **"  Lagos  "** (with two leading spaces and two trailing spaces). You want to clean it so it reads **"Lagos"** with no extra spaces.

Which function should you use?

options.text: =TRIM(B2)
=LEFT(B2,5)
=RIGHT(B2,5)

opt_b.message: =LEFT(B2,5) extracts the first 5 characters from the left. Because the string starts with two spaces, LEFT(B2,5) returns "  Lag" — the spaces are included and the full city name is cut off.

opt_c.message: =MID(B2,3,5) starts at position 3 (the first non-space character) and extracts 5 characters, returning "Lagos". This works for this specific string, but it relies on knowing exactly how many leading spaces there are. TRIM is the robust solution because it removes all leading and trailing spaces regardless of count.

opt_d.message: =RIGHT(B2,5) extracts the last 5 characters. Because the string ends with two spaces, RIGHT(B2,5) returns "gos  " — the trailing spaces are included.

correct.message: Correct! =TRIM(B2) removes all leading and trailing spaces from the text, returning "Lagos". TRIM also collapses multiple spaces between words to a single space, making it the standard tool for cleaning imported text.

incorrect.message: TRIM removes all spaces from a text value except for single spaces between words. It is the right tool when you need to clean leading or trailing spaces from imported data. LEFT, RIGHT, and MID extract characters by position — they do not remove spaces.

hints: TRIM is designed specifically to remove leading and trailing spaces from text.
LEFT and RIGHT extract characters from the start or end — they include any spaces that are there.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has order IDs in column A (e.g., **"LG-2001"**). Each order ID has a 2-letter prefix ("LG") followed by a hyphen and a 4-digit number.

In cell G2, write a formula using **LEFT** that extracts the first 2 characters of the order ID in A2 — the 2-letter prefix.

The expected result is **"LG"**.

correct.message: Correct! =LEFT(A2,2) extracts the first 2 characters of "LG-2001", returning "LG". LEFT(text, num_chars) always counts from the beginning of the string.

incorrect.message: Use =LEFT(A2,2). LEFT(text, num_chars) returns the first num_chars characters. "LG-2001" starts with "LG" — the first 2 characters.

hints: LEFT(text, num_chars) extracts characters from the left end of the string.
"LG-2001" has 7 characters. The first 2 characters are "LG".

public.prompt:
Cell G2 holds an order date. You want a formula that calculates how many **days** have elapsed between the order date in G2 and today's date.

Which formula uses **DATEDIF** to calculate how many days have elapsed between the order date in G2 and today's date?

options.text: =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"D")
=DATEDIF(TODAY(),G2,"D")
=DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"Y")
=TODAY()-G2

opt_b.message: if G2 is in the past, this returns a #NUM! error because DATEDIF requires start_date ≤ end_date.

opt_c.message: The unit "Y" returns the number of complete years, not days. To count days, use the unit "D".

opt_d.message: =TODAY()-G2 does return the number of days as a serial-number difference, and it works. However, the question asks for DATEDIF, which is the explicit function for date-difference calculations and makes the intent clearer. =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"D") is the correct DATEDIF form.

correct.message: Correct! =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"D") computes the number of complete days between the order date (G2) and today. DATEDIF syntax: DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit). The unit "D" returns days; "Y" would return complete years.

incorrect.message: DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit) requires the earlier date as start_date and the later date as end_date. TODAY() supplies today's date as the end_date. The unit "D" returns the number of days in the period.

hints: DATEDIF argument order: start_date first, end_date second. The order date (G2) is the start.
The unit controls what is counted: "D" = days, "Y" = complete years.

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has order dates in column G (rows 2–21). The starter file provides the order-date serial numbers for rows 2 and 3 in cells G2 and G3 (both are **45355**, representing 2024-03-04), and a fixed reference date in H1 (**45361**, representing 2024-03-10).

**Task 1 — days elapsed (fixed date):** In cell I2, write a DATEDIF formula that calculates the number of **days** (unit "D") between the order date in G2 and the reference date in H1. The result should be **6**.

**Task 2 — days for row 3:** In cell I3, write the same DATEDIF formula for G3. The result should also be **6**.

**Task 3 — age in years (TODAY):** In cell J2, write a formula using **DATEDIF** and **TODAY()** that calculates the number of complete **years** (unit "Y") between the order date in G2 and today's date. Use TODAY() as the end_date argument. Syntax: =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"Y").

solution_files.content:
H1: 45361
G2: 45355
G3: 45355
I2: =DATEDIF(G2,H1,"D")
I3: =DATEDIF(G3,H1,"D")
J2: =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"Y")

tests.message_on_fail: I2 should equal 6 (days from 2024-03-04 to 2024-03-10). Use =DATEDIF(G2,H1,"D") — G2 is the start_date, H1 is the end_date, "D" counts days.
I3 should equal 6 (days from 2024-03-04 to 2024-03-10). Use =DATEDIF(G3,H1,"D") — same pattern as I2 but referencing G3.
I2 must contain a DATEDIF formula.
J2 must contain a formula using both DATEDIF and TODAY(). Use =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"Y") — TODAY() supplies the current date as the end_date, and "Y" returns complete years.

correct.message: Well done! =DATEDIF(G2,H1,"D") correctly places the earlier date (G2) as start_date and the later date (H1) as end_date, with unit "D" for days. =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"Y") uses TODAY() as the end_date to compute the age in complete years — TODAY() returns today's date as a serial number, and "Y" counts complete years. Excel stores dates as serial numbers, so DATEDIF can subtract them to count days or years.

incorrect.message: For Tasks 1 and 2: Use =DATEDIF(G2,H1,"D") and =DATEDIF(G3,H1,"D"). The argument order is: start_date (earlier date), end_date (later date), unit ("D" for days). For Task 3: Use =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"Y") — TODAY() supplies today's date as the end_date, and "Y" returns the number of complete years.

hints: DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit): the earlier date goes first.
The unit "D" counts days. Use "Y" for complete years, "M" for complete months.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has city in column B (B2:B21), status in column E (E2:E21), and amount in column D (D2:D21).

You want the total amount for orders that are **both** from Lagos **and** have status Delivered. Which formula is correct?

options.text: =SUMIFS(D2:D21,B2:B21,"Lagos",E2:E21,"Delivered")
=SUMIF(D2:D21,"Lagos",E2:E21,"Delivered")
=SUMIFS(B2:B21,"Lagos",E2:E21,"Delivered",D2:D21)
=SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21)+SUMIF(E2:E21,"Delivered",D2:D21)

opt_b.message: SUMIF handles only one condition. Its syntax is SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]) — it takes one criteria range and one criterion. To apply two conditions at once, use SUMIFS.

opt_c.message: SUMIFS syntax is SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...). The sum_range (D2:D21) must come first. This formula puts the criteria ranges first and the sum_range last, which is the SUMIF order, not SUMIFS.

opt_d.message: Adding two SUMIF results double-counts orders that are both from Lagos AND Delivered. An order that meets both conditions is included in both SUMIF results, so the total is inflated. SUMIFS applies both conditions simultaneously to avoid double-counting.

correct.message: Correct! =SUMIFS(D2:D21,B2:B21,"Lagos",E2:E21,"Delivered") sums the amounts in D2:D21 where the city is Lagos AND the status is Delivered. SUMIFS syntax: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...).

incorrect.message: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, ...) applies multiple conditions simultaneously. The sum_range (D2:D21) comes first, then each criteria_range/criteria pair. SUMIF handles only one condition.

hints: SUMIFS (plural) handles multiple conditions; SUMIF (singular) handles one.
In SUMIFS, the sum_range is the first argument, followed by criteria_range/criteria pairs.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has delivery times in column C (C2:C21). You want to count how many deliveries took between 30 and 60 minutes (inclusive).

Which formula correctly counts deliveries where delivery_minutes >= 30 AND <= 60?

options.text: =COUNTIF(C2:C21,">=30 AND <=60")
=COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">=30 AND <=60")

opt_b.message: COUNTIF does not support compound criteria like ">=30 AND <=60" in a single criterion string. Each condition must be a separate criteria_range/criteria pair in COUNTIFS.

opt_c.message: COUNTIFS does not support compound criteria in a single string. ">=30 AND <=60" is not valid syntax. Use two separate criteria pairs: COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">=30",C2:C21,"<=60").

opt_d.message: This formula adds the count of deliveries >= 30 to the count of deliveries <= 60. Every delivery between 30 and 60 minutes is counted twice (once in each COUNTIF), so the result is inflated. COUNTIFS with two criteria counts each matching row exactly once.

correct.message: Correct! =COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">=30",C2:C21,"<=60") uses the same range (C2:C21) twice — once with the lower bound (">=30") and once with the upper bound ("<=60"). COUNTIFS counts only rows where both conditions are met simultaneously.

incorrect.message: To test a range condition (between two values), list the same range twice in COUNTIFS: COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">=30",C2:C21,"<=60"). Each criteria_range/criteria pair adds another condition that must be met. COUNTIF cannot handle two conditions at once.

hints: COUNTIFS allows you to use the same range more than once — once for each bound of the between condition.
Criteria containing comparison operators like >= and <= must be in quotation marks.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has city in column B (B2:B21) and order amount in column D (D2:D21).

In cell H1, write a SUMIF formula that totals the amounts for orders from **Lagos**. The city criterion is a text value, so it must be enclosed in double quotation marks.

The expected result is **28000**.

correct.message: Correct! =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21) sums the amounts in D2:D21 where the corresponding city in B2:B21 equals "Lagos". The text criterion "Lagos" is enclosed in double quotation marks, as required for text and expression criteria.

incorrect.message: Use =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21). SUMIF syntax: SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]). The criteria "Lagos" is a text value and must be in double quotation marks. Without quotes, Excel returns a #NAME? or #VALUE! error.

hints: SUMIF syntax: SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range). The range is where you check the condition.
Text criteria must be in double quotes: "Lagos". Number criteria do not need quotes.

public.prompt: A summary table has product categories across the top row (row 1) and quarterly totals in rows 2 and 3. You want to retrieve the Q2 total for the 'Logistics' category. Which formula correctly uses HLOOKUP to do this?

options.text: =HLOOKUP("Logistics", A1:D3, 3, FALSE)
=VLOOKUP("Logistics", A1:D3, 3, FALSE)
=HLOOKUP("Logistics", A1:D3, 2, FALSE)
=HLOOKUP(3, A1:D3, "Logistics", FALSE)

opt_b.message: VLOOKUP searches the leftmost column, not the top row. When the lookup values are in the top row, use HLOOKUP instead.

opt_c.message: The row_index_num 2 would return the Q1 row (row 2), not Q2. Q2 is in row 3, so row_index_num should be 3.

opt_d.message: In HLOOKUP the first argument is the lookup_value (the category name), not the row number. The row_index_num is the third argument.

correct.message: Correct! HLOOKUP searches the top row for 'Logistics', then returns the value from row 3 (row_index_num = 3), which is the Q2 row. FALSE forces an exact match.

incorrect.message: HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]) searches the top row for the lookup_value and returns the value from the row you specify. Row 1 is the header row, so Q2 data is in row 3.

hints: HLOOKUP is the horizontal counterpart of VLOOKUP: it scans across the top row instead of down the left column.
Count the rows from the top of the table: row 1 = headers, row 2 = Q1, row 3 = Q2.

public.prompt:
The **drivers** sheet has driver IDs in column A and driver names in column B. Cell A1 holds the lookup key **D01**.

**Task 1 — VLOOKUP:** In cell B1, write a VLOOKUP formula that looks up the value in A1 in the drivers sheet (columns A:B) and returns the driver name (column index 2). Use FALSE for an exact match.

**Task 2 — XLOOKUP:** In cell C1, write an XLOOKUP formula that looks up the value in A1 in drivers column A and returns the corresponding value from drivers column B.

tests.message_on_fail: B1 should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01. Check that your VLOOKUP uses A1 as the lookup value, drivers!A:B as the table, 2 as the column index, and 0 for exact match.
Cell B1 must contain a VLOOKUP formula.
C1 should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01. Check that your XLOOKUP uses A1 as lookup_value, drivers!A:A as lookup_array, and drivers!B:B as return_array.
Cell C1 must contain an XLOOKUP formula.

correct.message: Well done! Your VLOOKUP correctly uses the key column (A), the table range (drivers!A:B), column index 2, and 0 for exact match. Your XLOOKUP separates the lookup array (drivers!A:A) from the return array (drivers!B:B) and matches exactly by default.

incorrect.message: Check both formulas. VLOOKUP needs: lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, 0 (or FALSE). XLOOKUP needs: lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array. Both should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01.

hints: For VLOOKUP, the table_array must start with the column containing the lookup key (driver_id in column A of the drivers sheet).
For XLOOKUP, the lookup_array and return_array are separate arguments — you don't need a column index number.

public.prompt: A reference sheet has driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B. You want to look up driver ID 'D04' and return the driver's name. Which formula correctly uses INDEX/MATCH to do this?

options.text: =INDEX(A:A,MATCH("D04",B:B,0))
=VLOOKUP("D04",A:B,1,FALSE)
=INDEX(B:B,MATCH("D04",A:A,0))
=INDEX(A:A,MATCH("D04",B:B,1))

opt_b.message: VLOOKUP requires the lookup key to be in the leftmost column of the table. Here the key (driver ID) is in column B, which is to the right of the return value (driver name in column A). VLOOKUP cannot handle this layout.

opt_c.message: This formula looks up 'D04' in column A (driver names) and returns from column B (driver IDs) — the reverse of what you want. The INDEX array should be the column you want to return from (A), and the MATCH lookup_array should be the column containing the key (B).

opt_d.message: match_type 1 finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value and requires the array to be sorted ascending — it does not find an exact match. Use 0 for an exact match.

correct.message: Correct! INDEX(A:A, ...) targets the driver name column. MATCH('D04', B:B, 0) finds the exact position of 'D04' in the driver ID column. INDEX then returns the name at that row position.

incorrect.message: INDEX(array, row_num) returns the value at a given row in the array. MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, 0) finds the exact position of the key. Set INDEX's array to the column you want to return from (A), and MATCH's lookup_array to the column containing the key (B).

hints: Think of it in two steps: MATCH finds the row number of 'D04' in column B; INDEX uses that row number to fetch the name from column A.
match_type 0 means exact match — always use 0 when looking up a specific ID.

public.prompt:
The **drivers** sheet has driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B — the key column is to the **right** of the return column, so VLOOKUP cannot be used.

Cell C1 holds the lookup key **D01**.

In cell D1, write an INDEX/MATCH formula that:
- Uses INDEX on column A (the name column) as the array
- Uses MATCH with match_type 0 to find the exact position of C1 in column B
- Returns the driver name that corresponds to driver ID D01

tests.message_on_fail: D1 should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01. Check that INDEX uses A:A and MATCH uses B:B with match_type 0.
Cell D1 must contain a formula using both INDEX and MATCH.

correct.message: Excellent! INDEX(A:A, MATCH(C1, B:B, 0)) correctly handles the reversed layout: MATCH finds the row of D01 in column B, and INDEX returns the name from column A at that row.

incorrect.message: Remember: INDEX(array, row_num) returns a value from the array at the given row. MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, 0) returns the position of the lookup value. Set INDEX's array to A:A (names) and MATCH's lookup_array to B:B (IDs).

hints: Start with the outer function: INDEX(A:A, ...) — this says 'return a value from the driver name column'.
The MATCH inside finds the row: MATCH(C1, B:B, 0) — 'find the exact position of C1 in the driver ID column'.

public.prompt: Cell D10 contains the formula =D2+D3+D4+D5. The formula returns #VALUE!. You inspect the cells and find that D4 contains the text 'N/A' instead of a number. Which of the following correctly describes the cause and the fix?

options.text: The arithmetic + operator cannot add a text value; replacing the formula with =SUM(D2:D5) would fix it because SUM ignores text values and sums only the numeric ones.
The formula is referencing too many cells; reducing it to =D2+D3 would fix it.
The #VALUE! error means a cell reference is invalid (deleted or moved); re-entering the formula would fix it.
The + operator requires all cells to be formatted as Currency; reformatting D4 as Currency would fix it.

opt_b.message: The number of cells is not the issue. The problem is that D4 contains text. Even =D2+D4 alone would return #VALUE! because of the text in D4.

opt_c.message: A deleted or moved reference causes #REF!, not #VALUE!. #VALUE! indicates a type mismatch — the formula is trying to add a text value.

opt_d.message: Cell formatting does not change the underlying data type. D4 contains the text string 'N/A', not a number, regardless of how it is formatted. SUM would ignore it; the + operator cannot.

correct.message: Correct! The arithmetic + operator cannot handle text, so it returns #VALUE!. SUM(D2:D5) silently skips text values and sums only the numbers — the cleanest fix without removing the text cell.

incorrect.message: #VALUE! means the formula encountered a value of the wrong type. Here, D4 holds text ('N/A') and the + operator cannot add text. Switching to SUM resolves this because SUM ignores non-numeric cells.

hints: Think about what #VALUE! specifically means: something is wrong with the type of a value the formula is using.
SUM and the + operator behave differently when a cell contains text — one ignores it, the other fails.

public.prompt: Cell E5 contains =A5+B5 and returns #VALUE! because B5 holds text. Cell F5 contains =SUM(E5, C5, D5). What does F5 display?

options.text: #VALUE!
The sum of C5 and D5 only (SUM skips the error in E5)
0 (SUM treats errors as zero)
#REF!

opt_b.message: SUM ignores text values in its range, but it does not ignore error values such as #VALUE!. When a cell in SUM's range contains an error, SUM propagates that error.

opt_c.message: SUM does not treat errors as zero. It propagates them. Only text values (like 'N/A') are silently skipped by SUM; error values (like #VALUE!) cause SUM to return the same error.

opt_d.message: #REF! appears when a formula references an invalid cell (e.g., a deleted row). Here the reference is valid; the problem is that E5 itself contains a #VALUE! error, which SUM propagates.

correct.message: Correct! When SUM or AVERAGE reference a cell that already contains a #VALUE! error, they propagate that error rather than skipping it. SUM skips text values but not error values.

incorrect.message: SUM skips plain text values in its range, but it does not skip error values. If any cell in SUM's range contains #VALUE!, SUM returns #VALUE! too. This is error propagation.

hints: There is a difference between a cell containing the text 'N/A' and a cell containing the error #VALUE! — SUM treats them differently.
Think about what happens when SUM encounters an error cell versus a text cell.

public.prompt:
This workbook has three broken formulas.

**Fix 1 — #N/A in B8:** The VLOOKUP in B8 returns #N/A because the driver ID in A8 ('D0X') does not exist in the drivers sheet. Change A8 to the correct driver ID **D01** so the VLOOKUP finds a match and returns the driver name.

**Fix 2 — #REF! in C8:** The formula in C8 returns #REF! because it references a cell that is not valid. The formula should sum the values in E1 and F1 (which contain 100 and 200). Replace the #REF! formula in C8 with **=SUM(E1:F1)**.

**Fix 3 — #VALUE! in D9:** The formula =A9+B9+C9 in D9 returns #VALUE! because B9 contains the text 'N/A'. Replace the formula in D9 with one that sums A9:C9 but ignores the text value in B9.

tests.message_on_fail: B8 should return 'Amara Okafor'. Fix A8 to contain the correct driver ID 'D01' so the VLOOKUP finds a match.
C8 should return 300 (100 + 200). Replace the #REF! formula with =SUM(E1:F1).
D9 should return 300 (100 + 200, ignoring the text in B9). Replace the arithmetic formula with a SUM formula.
Cell D9 must use the SUM function to ignore the text value in B9.

correct.message: Well done! You fixed all three errors: correcting the misspelled driver ID resolved the #N/A (the lookup value now exists in the source data), replacing the #REF! formula resolved the invalid cell reference, and switching to SUM resolved the #VALUE! (SUM ignores text values, the + operator does not).

incorrect.message: Check all three fixes. For B8: the VLOOKUP returns #N/A because A8 contains 'D0X' which doesn't exist in the drivers sheet — change A8 to 'D01'. For C8: replace the #REF! formula with =E1+F1 to sum the values in E1 and F1. For D9: replace the + formula with =SUM(A9:C9) to ignore the text in B9.

hints: For the #N/A error: compare the value in A8 character by character with the driver IDs in the drivers sheet.
For the #REF! error: use SUM to add E1 (100) and F1 (200) to get 300.
