public.prompt: You are about to use Data > Remove Duplicates on your Orders sheet. Which statement best describes what you should do before running it, and why?

options.text: Copy the original data to another worksheet first, because Remove Duplicates permanently deletes the duplicate rows and the deletion cannot be undone once the workbook is saved and closed.
Sort the data by order_id first, because Remove Duplicates only works correctly on sorted data.
No preparation is needed; Remove Duplicates moves duplicates to a separate sheet so you can review them later.
Apply a filter to hide blank rows first, because Remove Duplicates will treat blank rows as duplicates and delete them.

opt_b.message: Remove Duplicates does not require sorted data. It compares rows based on the columns you select, regardless of their order in the sheet.

opt_c.message: Remove Duplicates does not move rows to another sheet — it permanently deletes them from the current sheet. There is no built-in review step.

opt_d.message: Remove Duplicates identifies duplicate rows based on the column values you select, not on whether rows are blank. Filtering blank rows first is not required and does not protect your original data.

correct.message: Correct! Remove Duplicates permanently deletes the duplicate rows. Copying the original data to another worksheet before running it gives you a backup in case you need to recover any rows.

incorrect.message: Remove Duplicates permanently deletes duplicate rows — there is no undo once the workbook is saved. The recommended precaution is to copy the original data to another worksheet before running the operation.

hints: Think about what 'permanently deleted' means for your data if you make a mistake.
The key word in the fact is 'permanently' — what safety step does that suggest?

public.prompt: The Orders table has order IDs in column A (A2:A21). When you run Data > Remove Duplicates and select only the **order_id** column in the Columns checklist, Excel compares rows using only that column. Type a formula in cell B1 that returns the order ID from the first data row (A2), confirming you can reference the cleaned data.

correct.message: Correct! =A2 returns 'LG-2001', the order ID in the first data row. After running Remove Duplicates on the order_id column, only unique order IDs remain — each row is identified by a distinct order ID.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell A2 directly. The order ID in the first data row is in cell A2 of the Orders sheet.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The first data row is row 2 (row 1 is the header). The order_id column is column A.

public.prompt: Column B of your Orders sheet contains entries like 'Lagos,Nigeria' — city and country combined in a single cell, separated by a comma. You want to split this into two separate columns. Which sequence of steps correctly uses Text to Columns to do this?

options.text: Select column B, choose Data > Text to Columns, select Delimited, check Comma as the delimiter, choose the destination, and select Finish.
Select column B, choose Data > Text to Columns, select Fixed Width, drag a break line between the city and country, and select Finish.
Select column B, choose Home > Find & Replace, enter ',' in Find, leave Replace blank, and select Replace All.
Select column B, choose Data > Remove Duplicates, check the Comma delimiter option, and select OK.

opt_b.message: Fixed Width is used when columns are separated by a consistent number of characters (like a fixed-width export), not by a delimiter character. Since the separator here is a comma, choose Delimited instead.

opt_c.message: Find & Replace removes or replaces text but does not split a cell into two columns. You need Text to Columns to distribute the split values into separate columns.

opt_d.message: Remove Duplicates removes repeated rows — it has nothing to do with splitting cell contents. Use Data > Text to Columns for splitting.

correct.message: Correct! Data > Text to Columns > Delimited > Comma splits 'Lagos,Nigeria' into two separate columns. The destination setting controls where the split values are placed.

incorrect.message: To split a column by a delimiter character (like a comma), use Data > Text to Columns, choose Delimited, select the delimiter (Comma), set the destination, and click Finish.

hints: The key word is 'delimited' — the data uses a specific character (comma) to separate the parts.
Text to Columns is on the Data tab, not the Home tab.

public.prompt: The location column (column B) in this Orders table stores city and country as a single value separated by a comma, for example 'Lagos,Nigeria'. After running Data > Text to Columns with Comma as the delimiter, the city part would move to column B and the country part to column C. Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the current combined value from B2, confirming you can read the source data before splitting.

correct.message: Correct! =B2 returns 'Lagos,Nigeria' — the combined city and country value in the first data row. After running Text to Columns with Comma as the delimiter, this cell would contain only 'Lagos' and the next column would contain 'Nigeria'.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell B2. The location column is column B, and the first data row is row 2.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The location column is column B; the first data row is row 2.

public.prompt: You are on the Summary sheet and need to pull a value from cell B1 on the Drivers sheet in the same workbook. Which formula is correct?

options.text: =Drivers!B1
=Drivers.B1
=[Drivers]B1
=Drivers:B1

opt_b.message: A dot (.) is not the separator between a sheet name and a cell reference. The correct separator is an exclamation point (!), giving Drivers!B1.

opt_c.message: Square brackets are used for workbook names in cross-workbook links (e.g., [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10), not for sheet names within the same workbook.

opt_d.message: A colon (:) is used to define a range (e.g., A1:B5), not to separate a sheet name from a cell reference. Use an exclamation point (!) instead.

correct.message: Correct! Within the same workbook, a cross-sheet reference uses the sheet name followed by an exclamation point and the cell address: Drivers!B1.

incorrect.message: A cross-sheet reference within the same workbook uses the sheet name, an exclamation point (!), and the cell address — for example, Drivers!B1. Square brackets are reserved for cross-workbook links.

hints: The separator between a sheet name and a cell address is the exclamation point (!).
Square brackets [ ] appear only in cross-workbook links, not in same-workbook references.

public.prompt: You need to write a formula on the Summary sheet that sums cells C10:C25 from a sheet named 'Annual' inside a separate open workbook called Budget.xlsx. Which formula is correct?

options.text: =SUM([Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25)
=SUM(Budget.xlsx!Annual!C10:C25)
=SUM('Budget.xlsx'!Annual!C10:C25)
=SUM(Annual!C10:C25)

opt_b.message: The workbook name must be enclosed in square brackets, not followed by an exclamation point directly. The correct syntax is [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25.

opt_c.message: Single quotes are used to enclose sheet names that contain spaces or numbers, not workbook file names. The workbook name goes in square brackets: [Budget.xlsx].

opt_d.message: This formula references the Annual sheet in the current workbook, not in Budget.xlsx. To reference another workbook, include the workbook name in square brackets before the sheet name.

correct.message: Correct! A cross-workbook link uses the workbook name in square brackets, followed by the sheet name, an exclamation point, and the cell range: [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25.

incorrect.message: A cross-workbook link (when the source workbook is open) uses the format [WorkbookName.xlsx]SheetName!CellRange. The workbook name goes in square brackets, not in quotes or with an extra exclamation point.

hints: Cross-workbook links have three parts: [workbook name], sheet name, and cell range — in that order.
Square brackets [ ] wrap the workbook file name; single quotes wrap sheet names that contain spaces.

public.prompt:
The workbook contains a sheet named **'2024Q1'** (the name starts with a number). In cell Z1 of the current sheet, write a formula that pulls the value from cell B4 on the '2024Q1' sheet.

Remember: when a sheet name starts with a number (or contains a space), it must be enclosed in single quotation marks in the reference.

tests.message_on_fail: Z1 should return 'Lagos' (the city in row 4 of the 2024Q1 sheet). Make sure you quote the sheet name: ='2024Q1'!B4

correct.message: Well done! ='2024Q1'!B4 correctly references cell B4 on the '2024Q1' sheet. The single quotes around the sheet name are required because the name starts with a number.

incorrect.message: The formula should be ='2024Q1'!B4. The sheet name '2024Q1' must be enclosed in single quotes because it starts with a number. Without the quotes, the spreadsheet cannot parse the reference.

hints: The syntax for a cross-sheet reference is SheetName!CellAddress. When the sheet name starts with a number (or has a space), wrap it in single quotes.
Try typing ='2024Q1'!B4 — the single quotes go around the entire sheet name, before the exclamation point.

public.prompt: You open the Sort dialog (Data > Sort) and configure two levels: Level 1 sorts by order_date Oldest to Newest, and Level 2 sorts by amount Largest to Smallest. What does this sort produce?

options.text: Rows are ordered by date first (oldest at the top); among rows that share the same date, they are further ordered by amount from largest to smallest.
Rows are ordered by amount first (largest at the top); among rows with the same amount, they are further ordered by date oldest to newest.
Both columns are sorted in the same direction because the Sort dialog applies a single direction to all levels.
The sort fails because you cannot mix ascending and descending directions in the same Sort dialog.

opt_b.message: In a multi-level sort, the level higher in the list is applied first. Level 1 (order_date) is applied before Level 2 (amount), so date is the primary sort key, not amount.

opt_c.message: Each level in the Sort dialog has its own independent Order dropdown. Level 1 can be Oldest to Newest while Level 2 is Largest to Smallest — they do not have to match.

opt_d.message: The Sort dialog fully supports mixing directions across levels. Each level has its own Order setting, so ascending and descending can be combined freely.

correct.message: Correct! The level higher in the Sort dialog list is applied first. Level 1 (order_date, Oldest to Newest) is the primary sort; Level 2 (amount, Largest to Smallest) is the tiebreaker for rows sharing the same date.

incorrect.message: In the Sort dialog, the level higher in the list is applied first. Level 1 (order_date) determines the primary order; Level 2 (amount) only applies within groups of rows that share the same date. Each level has its own independent Order setting.

hints: Think of the levels as a priority list: Level 1 is the main sort, Level 2 only breaks ties.
Each level in the Sort dialog has its own Order dropdown — they are independent of each other.

public.prompt: The Orders table has amounts in column D (D2:D21) and order dates in column G (G2:G21). To sort by amount from smallest to largest, you would select a cell in column D and choose **Sort Smallest to Largest** on the Data tab. The order with the smallest amount (1800) is in row 8 (order LG-2007). Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the amount from D8, confirming you can identify the value that would appear first after sorting.

correct.message: Correct! =D8 returns 1800 — the smallest amount in the dataset. After sorting column D from smallest to largest, this row would move to the top. For dates, you would use Sort Oldest to Newest or Sort Newest to Oldest instead.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell D8. D8 holds the amount for order LG-2007, which has the smallest amount (1800) in the dataset.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The amount column is column D; row 8 holds order LG-2007 with amount 1800.

public.prompt: You want to filter the Orders table to show only orders with an amount greater than 5000. Starting from a cell inside the table, what is the correct sequence of steps?

options.text: Select Data > Filter, click the filter arrow on the amount column header, choose Number Filters > Greater Than, enter 5000, and click OK.
Select Data > Sort, choose the amount column, set the order to Largest to Smallest, and click OK.
Select the amount column, choose Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Greater Than, enter 5000, and click OK.
Select Data > Filter, click the filter arrow on the amount column header, choose Text Filters > Greater Than, enter 5000, and click OK.

opt_b.message: Sorting reorders the rows but does not hide any rows. To show only rows meeting a condition, use Data > Filter, not Sort.

opt_c.message: Conditional Formatting highlights cells visually but does not hide rows. To show only rows where amount > 5000, use AutoFilter.

opt_d.message: Amount is a numeric column, so you should choose Number Filters, not Text Filters. Text Filters are for columns containing text values.

correct.message: Correct! Data > Filter turns on AutoFilter. Clicking the column header arrow and choosing Number Filters > Greater Than lets you enter a numeric threshold. Only rows meeting the condition are shown.

incorrect.message: To filter a range to rows meeting a condition: select Data > Filter, click the filter arrow on the column header, choose Number Filters (for numeric columns) or Text Filters (for text columns), select the comparison, enter the value, and click OK.

hints: Filtering hides rows that don't match — it's on the Data tab, not the Home tab.
Amount is a number, so use Number Filters, not Text Filters.

public.prompt: The Orders table has amounts in column D (D2:D21) and cities in column B (B2:B21). AutoFilter hides rows that do not match the filter criteria — it does not delete them. Clearing the filter restores all rows. Filters are additive: filtering by city 'Lagos' and then by amount > 3000 shows only rows where BOTH conditions are true. Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the amount from the first data row (D2), confirming you can read the unfiltered data.

correct.message: Correct! =D2 returns 4500 — the amount in the first data row. AutoFilter would hide rows that don't match your criteria, but D2 would still exist in the sheet. Clearing the filter would restore all rows, including any that were hidden.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell D2. The amount column is column D; the first data row is row 2.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The amount column is column D; the first data row is row 2.

public.prompt: The Orders table currently ends at row 21. A new delivery arrives and you type its order ID in cell A22. What happens to the table?

options.text: The table automatically expands to include row 22, applying the table style and structured references to the new row.
Nothing happens; you must manually resize the table by dragging its corner handle to include row 22.
Excel shows an error because the new row is outside the table boundary.
The table expands only if the new row contains data in every column.

opt_b.message: Manual resizing is not required. Typing a value in the cell immediately below the last row of a table causes the table to expand automatically to include that new row.

opt_c.message: No error occurs. Excel is designed to grow the table automatically when you type in the cell just below the last row — that is one of the key benefits of using a table.

opt_d.message: The table expands as soon as you type any value in the cell just below the last row, regardless of whether other columns in that row are filled in yet.

correct.message: Correct! Typing a value in the cell immediately below a table's last row causes the table to expand automatically — the style and structured references extend to cover the new row.

incorrect.message: Typing a value in the cell just below a table's last row automatically expands the table to include that row. No manual resizing is needed.

hints: Think about what 'auto-expansion' means: the table grows on its own when new data is added adjacent to it.
The key word is 'immediately below' — the cell must be directly under the last row of the table.

public.prompt: The Orders sheet has order data in rows 2 through 21 (20 orders total). In cell F1, write a formula that references the first order_id value (cell A2). This simple reference will help you verify that after formatting the range as a structured table, the reference behavior changes: the formula will automatically convert to a structured reference like =Orders[@order_id] when you click the cell.

correct.message: Correct! =A2 references the first order_id value (LG-2001). After formatting this range as a structured table named Orders (Home > Format as Table), Excel will display the formula as =A2 but you can also write it as =Orders[@order_id] using structured reference syntax. The table will auto-expand when you type a value in row 22, and structured references automatically adjust to include new rows.

incorrect.message: Write a formula that references cell A2: =A2. This references the first order_id value.

hints: Reference cell A2 directly: =A2
The order_id column is in column A, and the first data value is in row 2.

public.prompt: You have selected C2:C21 (the delivery_minutes column) and typed DeliveryTimes into the Name Box, then pressed Enter. Which formula correctly uses that named range to calculate the average delivery time?

options.text: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes)
=AVERAGE("DeliveryTimes")
=AVERAGE(C2:C21) — named ranges cannot be used in formulas
=DeliveryTimes.AVERAGE()

opt_b.message: Putting the name in quotes makes it a text string, not a range reference. Excel would return a #VALUE! error. Use the name without quotes: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

opt_c.message: Named ranges can absolutely be used in formulas. Once you define a name, you can type it directly in any formula in place of the cell range — for example =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

opt_d.message: That is not valid Excel syntax. To use a named range in a formula, simply type the name as the argument: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

correct.message: Correct! Once a name is defined, you use it directly in a formula as the argument — =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes) — without quotes and without any special syntax.

incorrect.message: A named range is used in a formula by typing the name directly as the argument, without quotes: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes). The name replaces the raw cell range C2:C21.

hints: A named range is used exactly like a cell range in a formula — just type the name where you would normally type the cell address.
No quotes, no dots, no special syntax — just the name: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

public.prompt: The delivery_minutes column is in column C (C2:C21). In cell G1, write a formula that returns the first delivery_minutes value (C2). After defining a named range FirstDelivery for C2 using the Name Box, you could write =FirstDelivery instead — but for this exercise, use the cell reference: =C2.

correct.message: Correct! =C2 returns 28 — the first delivery_minutes value. After defining a named range FirstDelivery for C2 (select C2, type FirstDelivery in the Name Box, press Enter), you could write =FirstDelivery for the same result. Named ranges make formulas more readable by replacing cell addresses with descriptive names.

incorrect.message: Write a formula that references cell C2: =C2. This returns the delivery_minutes value in the first data row.

hints: The formula is simply =C2, which references the cell in column C, row 2.
After defining a named range, you could write =FirstDelivery instead of =C2 — but for this exercise, use the cell reference.

public.prompt: You drag the city field into the Rows area of a PivotTable. Where does city appear in the finished PivotTable?

options.text: As Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable, with one row per city.
As Column Labels across the top of the PivotTable, with one column per city.
As a top-level report filter above the PivotTable.
As summarized numeric values in the body of the PivotTable.

opt_b.message: Column Labels appear when a field is placed in the Columns area, not the Rows area. A field in the Rows area appears as Row Labels on the left side.

opt_c.message: A top-level report filter appears when a field is placed in the Filters area. A field in the Rows area appears as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable.

opt_d.message: Summarized numeric values appear in the Values area. A field in the Rows area appears as Row Labels — one row per unique value of that field.

correct.message: Correct! A field placed in the Rows area appears as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable — one row for each unique value of that field (e.g., one row per city).

incorrect.message: The Rows area produces Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable. Each unique value of the field (e.g., each city name) gets its own row.

hints: Think about the four areas: Filters (top), Columns (top header), Rows (left side), Values (body numbers).
The Rows area places field values down the left side of the PivotTable as row labels.

public.prompt: You want a PivotTable that shows the total order amount for each city, with cities listed down the left and a single column of totals. Which field placement achieves this?

options.text: city in Rows area; amount in Values area.
city in Columns area; amount in Values area.
city in Values area; amount in Rows area.
city in Filters area; amount in Rows area.

opt_b.message: Placing city in the Columns area would spread city names across the top as column headers, not down the left as row labels. To list cities down the left, place city in the Rows area.

opt_c.message: The Values area holds numeric summaries, not category labels. city is a text field and should go in the Rows area; amount is numeric and should go in the Values area.

opt_d.message: The Filters area creates a top-level report filter, not row labels. To list cities down the left side, place city in the Rows area.

correct.message: Correct! city in the Rows area creates one row per city on the left side; amount in the Values area fills in the total for each city. That gives you the city-by-total layout you need.

incorrect.message: To list cities down the left with totals beside them, place city in the Rows area and amount in the Values area. Rows area → left-side labels; Values area → numeric summaries.

hints: Rows area = left-side labels (one row per unique value). Values area = numeric summaries in the body.
Match the field type to the area: text/category fields go in Rows or Columns; numeric fields go in Values.

public.prompt: A PivotTable with city in the Rows area and amount in the Values area would show the total amount for each city. In cell F1, write a formula that returns the total amount for Lagos orders — the value that would appear in the Lagos row of that PivotTable. Use SUMIF with the city range B2:B21, the criterion "Lagos", and the amount range D2:D21. (Note: SUMIF was covered in the earlier Text, Date, and Conditional Aggregation lesson.)

correct.message: Correct! =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21) returns 28000 — the total amount for Lagos orders. In a PivotTable with city in Rows and amount in Values, this is exactly the value that would appear in the Lagos row.

incorrect.message: Use SUMIF with three arguments: the city range (B2:B21), the criterion ("Lagos"), and the amount range (D2:D21). The formula is =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21).

hints: SUMIF takes three arguments: =SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range). The range is the city column, the criteria is "Lagos", and the sum_range is the amount column.
Make sure to put Lagos in double quotes inside the formula: =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21).

public.prompt: You add the status field (which contains text values: Delivered, Pending, Cancelled) to the Values area of a PivotTable. What summary function does Excel apply by default?

options.text: COUNT — because the field contains text values, not numbers.
SUM — because SUM is always the default for any field in the Values area.
AVERAGE — because Excel averages all values by default.
MAX — because Excel picks the largest value by default.

opt_b.message: SUM is the default only for numeric fields. When the field contains text values, Excel defaults to COUNT instead, because you cannot add text values together.

opt_c.message: AVERAGE is not the default for any field type. Excel defaults to SUM for numeric fields and COUNT for text fields.

opt_d.message: MAX is not the default. Excel defaults to SUM for numeric fields and COUNT for text fields.

correct.message: Correct! Excel defaults to COUNT for text fields in the Values area, because text values cannot be summed. For numeric fields it defaults to SUM.

incorrect.message: Excel uses COUNT as the default for text fields in the Values area (you cannot sum text), and SUM as the default for numeric fields.

hints: Ask yourself: can you add text values like 'Delivered' and 'Pending' together? If not, what would Excel do instead?
The rule is: numeric field → SUM by default; text field → COUNT by default.

public.prompt: A PivotTable currently shows the Sum of amount for each city. You want to change the Values area to show the Average of amount instead. In cell F1, write a formula that returns the average order amount across all 20 orders — the overall average that the PivotTable grand total row would show after switching to Average. Use AVERAGE with the range D2:D21.

correct.message: Correct! =AVERAGE(D2:D21) returns 4955 — the average order amount. After changing the PivotTable's Values field setting from Sum to Average, the grand total row would show this value.

incorrect.message: Use AVERAGE with the amount range: =AVERAGE(D2:D21). This returns the average order amount across all 20 orders.

hints: The AVERAGE function takes a range as its argument: =AVERAGE(D2:D21).
The amount column is column D, rows 2 through 21 (20 orders).

public.prompt: You have a table with two columns: city and total_amount. You want to create a bar chart to compare total order amounts across cities. Which axis encoding is correct for a bar chart?

options.text: Cities on the category axis; total_amount values represented by bar lengths on the value axis.
total_amount values on the category axis; cities represented by bar lengths on the value axis.
Cities on both axes, with total_amount shown as a colour gradient.
total_amount on both axes, with cities shown as data labels inside the bars.

opt_b.message: In a bar chart, categories (like city names) go on the category axis, and numeric values (like total_amount) are represented by bar lengths on the value axis — not the other way around.

opt_c.message: Bar charts do not use colour gradients to encode values. The category axis holds the category labels (cities) and the value axis holds the numeric values (total_amount), shown as bar lengths.

opt_d.message: Both axes cannot hold the same type of data. The category axis holds category labels (cities) and the value axis holds numeric values (total_amount) represented by bar lengths.

correct.message: Correct! In a bar chart, categories (city names) are organised along the category axis and numeric values (total_amount) are represented by bar lengths along the value axis.

incorrect.message: In a bar chart, categories go on the category axis and numeric values are shown as bar lengths on the value axis. Cities are the categories; total_amount is the value.

hints: A bar chart compares items: the items (categories) go on one axis, and their values (shown as bar lengths) go on the other.
Ask yourself: what am I comparing? Those are the categories. What am I measuring? That is the value axis.

public.prompt: The city_totals sheet has city names in column A (A2:A7) and total order amounts in column B (B2:B7). A bar chart of this data would place cities on the category axis and total amounts as bar lengths on the value axis. In cell C1, write a formula that returns the sum of all total_amount values in B2:B7 — the grand total that would appear in the chart's data range.

correct.message: Correct! =SUM(B2:B7) returns 99300 — the grand total of all city amounts. The bar chart would use B2:B7 as its value data, with each city's bar length proportional to its share of this total.

incorrect.message: Use SUM with the total_amount range: =SUM(B2:B7). The city_totals sheet has 6 cities in rows 2 through 7.

hints: The total_amount values are in column B, rows 2 through 7 (one row per city).
=SUM(B2:B7) adds up all six city totals.

public.prompt: Which of the following datasets is best suited for a line chart, and why?

options.text: Monthly revenue totals for Jan through Jun 2024 — because the data is time-ordered at equal intervals, making a line chart ideal for showing the trend.
Total order amounts by city — because cities are categories and a line chart connects them with a line.
A single order's delivery time — because a line chart can show a single data point.
Driver names and their order counts — because a line chart works for any two-column dataset.

opt_b.message: Cities are unordered categories, not time-ordered intervals. A line connecting unordered categories implies a trend that does not exist. A bar chart is better for comparing city totals.

opt_c.message: A single data point cannot show a trend. Line charts are suited to continuous data over time at equal intervals — multiple points that form a meaningful sequence.

opt_d.message: Driver names are unordered categories, not time-ordered intervals. Connecting them with a line would imply a trend that does not exist. A bar chart is more appropriate.

correct.message: Correct! Monthly revenue at equal time intervals (Jan, Feb, Mar…) is exactly the kind of data a line chart is designed for — it shows the trend across evenly spaced time points.

incorrect.message: Line charts are suited to continuous data over time at equal intervals (months, quarters, years). Unordered categories like cities or driver names should use a bar chart instead.

hints: Ask: is the horizontal axis a time sequence with equal spacing? If yes, a line chart works well.
A line connecting unordered categories (like cities) implies a trend that does not exist — that is a misuse of a line chart.

public.prompt: You have monthly revenue data: month labels in column A (Jan-2024 through Jun-2024) and total amounts in column B. You create a line chart using Insert > Recommended Charts. Which statement correctly describes the resulting chart?

options.text: Month labels are distributed evenly along the horizontal axis; revenue values are plotted on the vertical axis, connected by a line showing the trend over time.
Revenue values are distributed along the horizontal axis; month labels appear on the vertical axis.
Both axes show revenue values; month labels appear as data point labels on the line.
The chart shows bars instead of a line because monthly data always produces a bar chart.

opt_b.message: In a line chart, category data (month labels) is distributed along the horizontal axis and value data (revenue) is plotted on the vertical axis — not the other way around.

opt_c.message: The horizontal axis holds category data (month labels), not revenue values. Revenue values are plotted on the vertical axis.

opt_d.message: Monthly data does not automatically produce a bar chart. When you select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts, Excel recommends a line chart for evenly spaced time-series data.

correct.message: Correct! In a line chart, category data (month labels) is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis and value data (revenue) is plotted on the vertical axis, with points connected by a line.

incorrect.message: In a line chart, the horizontal axis holds the category data (month labels) evenly spaced, and the vertical axis holds the value data (revenue). The line connects the data points to show the trend.

hints: Remember: horizontal axis = category data (months); vertical axis = value data (revenue).
The line connects the data points in order, showing how revenue changes from month to month.

public.prompt: The monthly_summary sheet has month labels in column A (A2:A7, Jan-2024 through Jun-2024) and total order amounts in column B (B2:B7). A line chart of this data would place months evenly along the horizontal axis and revenue values on the vertical axis. In cell C1, write a formula that returns the sum of all monthly totals in B2:B7 — the grand total across all six months.

correct.message: Correct! =SUM(B2:B7) returns 1976900 — the total revenue across all six months. The line chart would use B2:B7 as its value data, with each month's point plotted on the vertical axis.

incorrect.message: Use SUM with the total_amount range: =SUM(B2:B7). The monthly_summary sheet has 6 months in rows 2 through 7. To create a line chart from this data, select A1:B7, then go to Insert → Recommended Charts and choose the Line chart option.

hints: The total_amount values are in column B, rows 2 through 7 (one row per month).
=SUM(B2:B7) adds up all six monthly totals.

public.prompt: You have city order totals for 6 cities, all amounts positive. You select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts to create a pie chart. Which statement correctly describes the resulting chart?

options.text: Each city appears as a slice; each slice's size is proportional to that city's share of the total amount; all slices together represent 100% of total revenue.
Each city appears as a bar; bar lengths represent the city's total amount; the chart shows absolute values, not proportions.
Each city appears as a point on a line; the line shows how city totals change from city to city.
Each city appears as a slice, but slices are equal in size because pie charts do not encode values.

opt_b.message: That describes a bar chart, not a pie chart. A pie chart shows proportions: each slice's size represents that category's share of the whole, and all slices together equal 100%.

opt_c.message: That describes a line chart. A pie chart shows proportions as slices of a circle, not points on a line.

opt_d.message: Pie chart slices are not equal — they are sized proportionally to each category's value. A slice for Lagos (the largest city total) would be larger than a slice for Enugu (the smallest).

correct.message: Correct! In a pie chart, each category is a slice sized proportionally to its share of the total. All slices together represent 100% of the data series.

incorrect.message: A pie chart shows proportions: each slice represents one category's share of the whole, sized proportionally to its value. All slices together equal 100%.

hints: The key word for pie charts is 'proportional' — each slice's size shows that category's fraction of the total.
All slices together must equal 100% of the data series — that is what makes it a 'pie'.

public.prompt: The city_totals sheet has city names in A2:A7 and total amounts in B2:B7. A pie chart is appropriate here because there is only one data series, all values are positive, and the number of categories does not exceed seven. In cell C1, write a formula that counts the number of city labels in A2:A7 — confirming that the category count is within the pie chart eligibility limit.

correct.message: Correct! =COUNTA(A2:A7) returns 6 — there are 6 cities, which is within the seven-category limit for pie charts. With all positive values and a single data series, this dataset meets all pie chart eligibility conditions.

incorrect.message: Use COUNTA to count the city labels in A2:A7: =COUNTA(A2:A7). COUNTA counts non-empty cells, including text labels.

hints: COUNTA counts all non-empty cells, including text. Use it to count the city names in A2:A7.
The pie chart eligibility rule says no more than seven categories. COUNTA(A2:A7) tells you how many categories there are.

public.prompt: You want to highlight all cells in the delivery_minutes column (C2:C21) that contain values below 30, using a red fill. Which sequence of steps achieves this?

options.text: Select C2:C21 → Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than → enter 30 → choose a red fill format.
Select C2:C21 → Insert → Conditional Formatting → Less Than → enter 30 → choose a red fill format.
Select C2:C21 → Home → Format Cells → Conditional → Less Than → enter 30 → choose a red fill format.
Select C2:C21 → Data → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than → enter 30 → choose a red fill format.

opt_b.message: Conditional Formatting is not on the Insert tab. It is on the Home tab, in the Styles group. The correct path is Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than.

opt_c.message: There is no Conditional option inside Format Cells. Conditional Formatting is a separate command on the Home tab: Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than.

opt_d.message: Conditional Formatting is not on the Data tab. It is on the Home tab, in the Styles group. The correct path is Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than.

correct.message: Correct! The path is Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than → enter 30 → choose the red fill format. The rule then applies the format automatically to any cell below 30.

incorrect.message: Conditional Formatting is on the Home tab (not Insert or Data). The path is: Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than → enter the threshold → choose the format.

hints: Conditional Formatting lives on the Home tab, in the Styles group — not on Insert or Data.
The Highlight Cells Rules submenu contains comparison commands like Less Than, Greater Than, and Equal To.

public.prompt: You want to highlight all cells in the delivery_minutes column (C2:C21) that contain values less than 30. In cell F1, write a formula that returns TRUE if the value in C2 is less than 30, and FALSE otherwise. This formula logic is what a conditional formatting rule would use to determine which cells to highlight.

correct.message: Correct! =C2<30 returns TRUE because 28 is less than 30. In conditional formatting, you would use Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than to apply this logic to the entire range C2:C21, highlighting all cells where the value is less than 30.

incorrect.message: Write a formula that compares C2 to 30: =C2<30. This returns TRUE if the value is less than 30, FALSE otherwise.

hints: Use the less than operator (<) to compare C2 to 30.
The formula should return TRUE or FALSE based on whether the value meets the condition.

public.prompt: You want to restrict the delivery_minutes column so that only whole numbers between 1 and 300 can be entered. In the Data Validation dialog, which settings achieve this?

options.text: Allow: Whole Number; Data: between; Minimum: 1; Maximum: 300.
Allow: Decimal; Data: between; Minimum: 1; Maximum: 300.
Allow: List; Source: 1,300.
Allow: Text Length; Data: between; Minimum: 1; Maximum: 300.

opt_b.message: Decimal allows fractional numbers (e.g., 45.5). To restrict to whole numbers only, choose Whole Number, not Decimal.

opt_c.message: List creates a dropdown with specific values. To allow any whole number in a range, choose Whole Number with a between condition and set the minimum and maximum.

opt_d.message: Text Length restricts the number of characters in a text entry, not the numeric value. To restrict to whole numbers between 1 and 300, choose Whole Number with a between condition.

correct.message: Correct! Allow: Whole Number; Data: between; Minimum: 1; Maximum: 300 restricts the cell to whole numbers in that range. Any entry outside the range triggers the error message.

incorrect.message: To allow only whole numbers between 1 and 300, set Allow to Whole Number, Data to between, Minimum to 1, and Maximum to 300.

hints: The Allow dropdown determines the type of data permitted. For whole numbers, choose Whole Number (not Decimal or Text Length).
The Data dropdown sets the condition (between, greater than, less than, etc.). For a range, choose between and set the minimum and maximum.

public.prompt: A colleague wants to restrict the status column so that users can only enter one of three values: Delivered, Pending, or Cancelled. Which validation type should they choose?

options.text: List — because it creates a dropdown with the exact allowed values, preventing any other entry.
Whole Number — because the status values can be coded as numbers (1, 2, 3).
Text Length — because each status value has a specific character count.
Decimal — because status values can be represented as decimal codes.

opt_b.message: Whole Number restricts entries to numeric values within a range. It cannot enforce specific text values like 'Delivered'. Use List to restrict entries to a fixed set of text options.

opt_c.message: Text Length restricts the number of characters, not the specific text. 'Delivered' (9 chars) and 'Cancelled' (9 chars) have the same length, so Text Length cannot distinguish between them. Use List instead.

opt_d.message: Decimal restricts entries to numeric values. It cannot enforce specific text values like 'Pending'. Use List to create a dropdown with the allowed text values.

correct.message: Correct! List validation creates a dropdown showing the allowed values (Delivered, Pending, Cancelled) and prevents any other entry. It is the right choice when you need to restrict input to a fixed set of text options.

incorrect.message: When you need to restrict input to a fixed set of text values, use List validation. It creates a dropdown with the allowed options and blocks any other entry.

hints: List validation is designed for exactly this scenario: a fixed set of allowed values shown as a dropdown.
Whole Number and Decimal are for numeric ranges; Text Length is for character counts. None of those can enforce specific text values.

public.prompt: You want to restrict the status column (E2:E21) so that users can only enter Delivered, Pending, or Cancelled. In cell G1, write a formula that returns TRUE if the value in E2 is one of these three allowed values, and FALSE otherwise. Use arithmetic and comparison operators: =(E2="Delivered")+(E2="Pending")+(E2="Cancelled")>0

correct.message: Correct! =(E2="Delivered")+(E2="Pending")+(E2="Cancelled")>0 returns TRUE because E2 contains "Delivered", which is one of the allowed values. Each comparison returns 1 (TRUE) or 0 (FALSE); adding them gives a count of matches, and >0 checks if at least one match exists. In data validation, you would use Data → Data Validation → Allow: List with Source set to Delivered,Pending,Cancelled to create a dropdown that restricts entry to these three values.

incorrect.message: Use arithmetic and comparison operators to check if E2 equals any of the three allowed values: =(E2="Delivered")+(E2="Pending")+(E2="Cancelled")>0. Each comparison returns 1 or 0; adding them counts matches; >0 checks if any match exists.

hints: Each comparison like E2="Delivered" returns TRUE (1) or FALSE (0). Adding three comparisons counts how many match.
